questions.solution_text:
$f(x) = 5+2\sin x$, so $f'(x) = 2\cos x$.
$\int \dfrac{\cos x}{5+2\sin x}\,dx$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{2\cos x}{5+2\sin x}\,dx$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln|5+2\sin x| + C$

questions.question_text: Which of these integrals **cannot** be found using $\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$?

options.why: The numerator is half of $f'(x) = 2x$, and a constant adjustment makes the rule work.
The numerator is exactly $f'(x) = 6x^{5}$, so the rule applies directly.
The numerator is exactly $f'(x) = 4x+3$, so the rule applies directly.

questions.solution_text:
For $\int \dfrac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+4}\,dx$, $f(x) = x^{2}+4$ and $f'(x) = 2x$.
$\dfrac{x^{2}}{2x} = \dfrac{x}{2}$, which still contains $x$, so the numerator is not a constant multiple of $f'(x)$.
Only a constant factor may be adjusted for, so the rule cannot be used here.
